## What the files look like

Each HMD bulk file holds every population in one whitespace-separated
table.  The first line names the series and gives its "Last modified"
stamp, the second is blank, and the third is the column header.  Missing
values are written as a single dot, and the oldest age group is written
`110+` (the open interval: everyone aged 110 or more).

```{python}
#| label: d2-setup
#| code-summary: "Chapter setup"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mdmx import artifacts, data, latex, lifetable, plotting, provenance
from mdmx.config import params

provenance.start_chapter("d2-ingest")
plotting.use_style()
P = params()
release = artifacts.load("hmd_release")
source = data.hmd_source(P.data.hmd_release)
```

```{python}
#| label: d2-peek
#| code-summary: "Print the first lines of the female life-table file"
with data.open_member(source, data.HMD_MEMBERS["lt_female"]) as fh:
    for _ in range(5):
        print(fh.readline().rstrip())
```

## Reading the files

`mdmx.data.ingest_life_tables()` reads the female and male files with
pandas (splitting on runs of whitespace and treating `.` as missing),
converts `110+` to the integer 110, and stacks the two sexes into one
**long** table with one row per population × sex × year × age.  A long table
is the natural format for a data pipeline: every filter, join and summary is
a one-liner, and each row is one fact.  `ingest_deaths_exposures()` does the
same for the death counts and exposures, which are published with female,
male and total columns side by side and are reshaped to the same long form.

Both tables are saved as **artefacts** — Parquet files in `work/companion/artifacts/`
with a provenance record that names their input (the verified release) — so
later chapters load them in a fraction of a second instead of re-parsing
200 MB of text.

```{python}
#| label: d2-ingest
#| code-summary: "Parse the four HMD files into long tables (cached)"

def _ingest():
    lt, lt_report = data.ingest_life_tables(source)
    de, de_report = data.ingest_deaths_exposures(source)
    return {"lt": lt, "de": de, "report": {**lt_report, **de_report}}

raw = artifacts.stage("hmd_raw", _ingest, inputs=["hmd_release"], code=[_ingest, data],
                      desc="HMD 1x1 period life tables, deaths and exposures, long format")
lt_raw, de_raw = raw["lt"], raw["de"]

for member, rep in raw["report"].items():
    print(f"{member:<45s} {rep['rows']:>9,} rows   [{rep['title'][:60]}]")
print()
print(lt_raw.head())
```

```{python}
#| label: d2-counts
#| code-summary: "Basic counts"
n_pops = lt_raw["pop"].nunique()
n_tables = lt_raw.groupby(["pop", "sex", "year"], observed=True).ngroups
first, last = int(lt_raw["year"].min()), int(lt_raw["year"].max())
missing_rows = int(lt_raw[["mx", "qx", "ax"]].isna().any(axis=1).sum())

latex.report("dataNPopsHMD", n_pops, desc="Populations in the HMD release")
latex.report("dataNTablesHMD", n_tables, desc="Sex-specific 1x1 period life tables in the release")
latex.report("dataFirstYear", first, text=str(first), desc="First calendar year in the HMD")
latex.report("dataLastYear", last, text=str(last), desc="Last calendar year in the HMD")
print(f"{n_pops} populations, {n_tables:,} sex-specific life tables, years {first}–{last}")
print(f"{missing_rows:,} rows contain a missing value (all in the tables listed in chapter d3)")
```

## A first look

The figures in this section show the data **as published by the HMD**,
before any curation.  They use the 48 populations retained for the analysis
(the two civilian-only duplicate series are left out, see chapter d1).

```{python}
#| label: d2-included
#| code-summary: "Restrict the descriptive figures to the retained populations"
pops = artifacts.load("populations")
keep = set(pops.loc[pops["included"] == "yes", "code"])
names = dict(zip(pops["code"], pops["name"]))
lt48 = lt_raw[lt_raw["pop"].isin(keep)]
e0 = (lt48[lt48["age"] == 0][["pop", "sex", "year", "ex"]]
      .rename(columns={"ex": "e0"}).reset_index(drop=True))
```

### Coverage

The HMD is **ragged**: Sweden's series begins in 1751, but many populations
enter only in the second half of the twentieth century.  This raggedness is
the central data problem the decomposition has to deal with (chapter 04).

```{python}
#| label: fig-s1-coverage
#| fig-cap: "HMD temporal coverage by population. Each coloured cell indicates that a 1×1 period life table is available for that population-year. Populations are sorted by the first year of available data."
#| fig-height: 7
cov = (e0[e0["sex"] == "female"].assign(v=1)
       .pivot_table(index="pop", columns="year", values="v", fill_value=0))
cov = cov.loc[cov.idxmax(axis=1).sort_values().index]           # sort by first year
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
ax.imshow(cov.to_numpy(), aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest",
          cmap=plt.matplotlib.colors.ListedColormap(["#f0f0f0", "#2171b5"]),
          extent=(cov.columns[0] - 0.5, cov.columns[-1] + 0.5, len(cov) - 0.5, -0.5))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(cov)), [names[p] for p in cov.index], fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.grid(False)
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-coverage")
plt.show()
latex.report("dataNPopsBeforeNineteenHundred", int((cov.idxmax(axis=1) < 1900).sum()),
             desc="Retained populations whose series start before 1900")
latex.report("dataNPopsFromNineteenThirtyThree", int((cov.idxmax(axis=1) >= 1933).sum()),
             desc="Retained populations whose series start in 1933 or later")
```

### Life expectancy at birth

```{python}
#| label: fig-s1-e0-trends
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy at birth over time for all retained HMD populations, by sex. Thin lines: individual populations; bold line: the median across populations in each year. Sharp dips mark wars and pandemics."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, sex in zip(axes, data.SEXES):
    sub = e0[e0["sex"] == sex]
    for _, g in sub.groupby("pop"):
        ax.plot(g["year"], g["e0"], color=plotting.COLORS[sex], alpha=0.15, lw=0.6)
    med = sub.groupby("year")["e0"].median()
    ax.plot(med.index, med.to_numpy(), color=plotting.COLORS[sex], lw=2, label="Median")
    ax.set_title(sex.title())
    ax.set_xlabel("Year")
    ax.legend(loc="lower right")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$e_0$ (years)")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-e0-trends")
plt.show()
```

### The age pattern of mortality

The probability of dying, $q_x$, has the familiar U (or J) shape: high in
infancy, lowest around age 10, then rising roughly exponentially with age.
The logit transform, $\operatorname{logit}(q) = \log\{q/(1-q)\}$, maps
probabilities onto the whole real line; on that scale the old-age rise is
close to linear, variability is more even across ages, and differences
between schedules are additive — which is why the whole analysis works with
$\operatorname{logit}(q_x)$ (paper §2.2, "The quantity modelled").

```{python}
#| label: d2-selection
#| code-summary: "Schedules used to illustrate the age pattern"
# Russia's HMD series ends in 2014, so its most recent table is used.
SELECTION = [("SWE", 1800), ("SWE", 1900), ("SWE", 2020), ("JPN", 2020),
             ("USA", 2020), ("RUS", 2014)]
def schedule(pop, year, sex):
    s = lt48[(lt48["pop"] == pop) & (lt48["year"] == year) & (lt48["sex"] == sex)
             & (lt48["age"] <= P.data.age_max)].sort_values("age")
    return s["age"].to_numpy(), s["qx"].to_numpy()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s1-qx-profiles
#| fig-cap: "Age-specific probability of dying (q_x, log scale) for selected populations and years: high infant mortality, a childhood minimum, and an approximately exponential increase at older ages."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, sex in zip(axes, data.SEXES):
    for pop, year in SELECTION:
        age, q = schedule(pop, year, sex)
        ax.semilogy(age, np.clip(q, 1e-6, None), lw=1.1, label=f"{names[pop]} {year}")
    ax.set_title(sex.title()); ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$q_x$ (log scale)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-qx-profiles")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s1-logit-qx
#| fig-cap: "The same schedules on the logit scale. Above age 40 the rise is close to linear (the Gompertz law); the transform stabilises variance and makes differences between schedules additive."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, sex in zip(axes, data.SEXES):
    for pop, year in SELECTION:
        age, q = schedule(pop, year, sex)
        ax.plot(age, lifetable.logit(q, P.data.q_min), lw=1.1, label=f"{names[pop]} {year}")
    ax.set_title(sex.title()); ax.set_xlabel("Age")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"logit$(q_x)$")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-logit-qx")
plt.show()
```

### The sex differential

On the logit scale the male–female difference
$\operatorname{logit}(q^{m}_x) - \operatorname{logit}(q^{f}_x)$ is a log odds
ratio.  Positive values mean higher male mortality, which is the case at
almost every age; the excess is largest in young adulthood and has grown
since the nineteenth century.

```{python}
#| label: fig-s1-sex-diff
#| fig-cap: "Male–female difference in logit mortality by age, Sweden, selected years. Values above zero indicate excess male mortality."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
years = [1800, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2000, 2020]
for year, colour in zip(years, plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 0.9, len(years)))):
    age, qf = schedule("SWE", year, "female")
    _, qm = schedule("SWE", year, "male")
    ax.plot(age, lifetable.logit(qm) - lifetable.logit(qf), color=colour, lw=1.2, label=str(year))
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylabel(r"logit$(q_x^{m})$ − logit$(q_x^{f})$")
ax.legend(ncol=3, fontsize=8)
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-sex-diff")
plt.show()
```
